newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: PROBE BEGINS INTO DEMOLITION TRAGEDY
The task of unravelling the cause of a fatal accident at the demolition of two Canberra buildings is underway.
A 12-year-old girl was killed and at least eight people injured yesterday at the implosion of the buildings on the site of the former Royal Canberra Hospital.
Debris from the falling buildings fell around spectators who had been kept at least 200 metres away.
Police say the girl was standing with her parents and brothers about 450 metres from the demolition when she was killed.
Debris was found up to 650 metres away.
Detective Constable Mark Johnsen said he's surprised more people weren't hurt.
He said a coronial inquiry will be held.
WA LIBS: PROSSER DID "NOTHING IMPROPER"
Former Federal Small Business Minister Geoff Prosser did nothing wrong, according to the deputy branch leader of the West Australian Liberals.
Prosser resigned on Friday after weeks of allegations of a conflict of interest between his ministerial duties and private business interests.
WA's deputy branch leader Colin Barnett said Mr Prosser's only crime was that he was such a successful businessman.
Barnett has told ABC Radio it was a harsh punishment for him to have to resign.
"Geoff Prosser's learnt a fairly harsh lesson, he's young enough and enthusiastic enough to bounce back, and I think he will because he's committed no misdemeanour at all," he said.
"There is nothing improper or wrong in what he's done, he's simply kept some association with his business affairs, and that was contrary to what John Howard had asked of ministers."
HOPES THAT AID WILL GET TO PHNOM PENH RESIDENTS
Aid workers in Cambodia hope they will be able to get help tomorrow to several thousand residents cut off in Phnom Penh since the coup that left Hun Sen in sole command of the government.
The people affected are living in areas hit by shelling during the coup and, since then, quarantined by the Hun Sen forces.
Many have lost their homes due to artillery fire.
Alan Crouch from Australian Red Cross said workers tried to get aid to the Phnom Penh residents over the weekend, but they were denied access by Hun Sen-loyal soldiers.
Meanwhile, in Australia, Federal Cabinet will today consider whether Australia should formally recognise Cambodia's new regime under Hun Sen.
Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said the government will discuss that, and Australia's foreign aid to Cambodia over the next couple of days.
COAL CARRIER TO BE REFLOATED ON HIGH TIDE TONIGHT
An attempt will be made tonight to refloat a bulk carrier stuck on a sandbank in the Torres Strait, with a tug on its way to the scene from Port Moresby, in Papua New Guinea.
No attempt will be made to refloat the vessel until the tide is higher and the tug is in place, expected to be about 10 o'clock tonight.
The carrier was laden with coal when it ran aground in the tidal waters of the Prince of Wales Channel in the Torres Strait on Saturday night.
No coal or oil has been spilt, but an invesitgation has begun.
The Bombay registered carrier was on its way to India when it struck the sandbank.
POSSIBLE CLASS ACTION ON FLU-LIKE DISEASE
Lawyers representing two meatworkers from the southern Queensland city of Toowoomba who allegedly contracted Q Fever, have warned it may be quite widspread.
The disease, which causes flu-like symptoms, is transmitted through contact with meat and animal body parts.

Lawyers, who have started proceedings in the Brisbane Supreme Court seeking compensation for loss and damage, are now calling on other meatworkers and inspectors who believe they have had the disease to come forward.
Solicitor Barry Roche, himself a former meat inspector, said they believe the brucellosis-type disease could be quite widespread.
His firm, Watling Roche, has advertised for meatworkers and inspectors affected by the disease to contact it, with a view to launching a possible class action.
AMERICAS' CUP BACK AFTER PANELBEATING
International yachting's oldest trophy arrives back in New Zealand today, but it will be some time before the public can view it again.
The Americas' Cup will be privately returned to the Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron in Auckland following its restoration in London.
The trophy was badly damaged several months ago in a sledgehammer attack, allegedly by a Maori activist who is facing trial over the incident.
The Cup will not go on public display until a reinforced display case is installed in the yacht club.
